newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil markets buzz with daily political 'soap'.
newsitem.headline: Brazil markets buzz with daily political 'soap'.

text.p: A vote-buying scandal that erupted in the press this week has financial markets buzzing with speculation, returning Brazil to an era when rumours about tomorrow's headlines steered investor decision-making.

A series of exclusive reports in Folha de Sao Paulo alleges Cabinet-level ties to a cash-for-votes scam that purportedly seeks to guarantee President Fernando Henrique Cardoso a second term in office.
Most political and market analysts doubt whether Cardoso himself will ever be tied directly to any wrongdoing. But nobody is betting the farm until the series of Folha stories has run its course.

"Supposedly, the worst will come out on Sunday, but we'll have to wait and see," said Tina Vandersteel, a fixed-income and political analyst at JP Morgan in Brazil. "If nothing more serious comes out, then I think we can get back to normal pretty soon."

Brokerage houses in Brazil have been flooded with calls from nervous overseas investors since Folha published its first story on Tuesday. The story cited a taped conversation with a lawmaker who says he received $190,000 cash to vote for a controversial bill that would allow re-election of Cardoso and other executive office holders.

On Wednesday and Thursday, the paper ran reports linking Communications Minister Sergio Motta, a close Cardoso ally, to the alleged scam. Motta has denied the allegations and the lawmaker said he was joking when he spoke about the sale of his vote.
Still, the reports have rocked the capital of Brasilia and financial markets -- both of which are uncertain about the reach of the political fallout.

The Sao Paulo stock exchange fell 3.4 percent on Wednesday, its largest one-day drop this year. Stocks rebounded on Thursday but lost most of the 2.0 percent gain late in the session on rumours that more damaging stories would be printed on Friday. Rumours about upcoming vote-scam headlines have circulated about an hour before the market close every day, pressuring prices.
Market watchers do not think the scandal is strong enough to prevent a second term for Cardoso, but they fear it could further delay key economic reforms now stuck in Congress.
As a result, traders and analysts say they are awaiting the next day's headlines in a way millions of Brazilians anticipate the next episode of one of the nation's gripping, late-night melodramas.
An internal memo about the scandal at a leading investment bank on Thursday was titled "Re-election Novela (Soap Opera): Day Three."

One observer referred to Folha's slow yet deliberate release of a new bit of information each day as a "media striptease," with market players at the edge of their seats, waiting to see the next titillating piece of evidence revealed.
The whole affair has reminded Brazilians of a not-so-distant past when financial markets ignored economic fundamentals and took their cue from speculation over tomorrow's headlines.

The steady downfall of former President Fernando Collor de Melo was carried out through exclusive stories each week in the nation's leading weekly news magazine Veja. During the week, the market would trade based on speculation about what Veja might turn up in its next edition.
Collor was eventually forced to resign in 1992 amid corruption allegations and impeachment proceedings.
